title: Trust Without Consensus in Federated IoT Systems: Relational Governance for Pluralistic Federated IoT
content: Federated learning enables collaboration among participants whose data remain locally held. Its capacity to accommodate heterogeneous data does not, by itself, determine whether participants are authorized to exchange knowledge or adopt a common policy. This paper develops a conceptual framework for federations whose participants face different mandatory requirements and accountability obligations. It distinguishes statistical, operational, and normative heterogeneity, then derives three design principles: contextual non-substitutability, non-compositionality, and legitimate non-convergence. A formal account separates the feasibility of a shared policy from the permissibility of knowledge transfer. Relational trust agreements specify the parties and affected subjects, the knowledge exchanged, its purpose, and the conditions governing its use. These agreements support a proposed architecture, Relationally Governed Pluralistic Federated Intelligence, that permits selective cooperation, context-specific policies, and withdrawal subject to safe fallback arrangements. An industrial IoT illustration shows why similarity of sensor data cannot establish compatibility of obligations. The paper distinguishes analytical claims from empirical hypotheses and specifies comparisons with personalized, constrained, and context-conditioned learning systems. Its contribution is an account of how authority, evidence, and contestability can govern learning across independently accountable contexts.
